    10	## How loops and reductions call the library
    11	
    12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
    13	
    14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
    15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
    16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
    17	
    18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
    19	
    20	## The curator's decisions on the library
    21	
    22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
    23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
    24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
    25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. The element type is written before the generators, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. In the library, write it, as its own sites do. For a call without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, or else its body's type (`revival-changes.md`, "Reductions and comprehensions"). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).

So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).

    95	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
    96	- A superscript is `^` and what follows it, as the exponent in `x^2` or the transpose `^T`. It can follow a dotted access: `p.wq^T` is `(p.wq)^T`. After a call or a subscript, parenthesise first, as `(f(x))^T` and `(x[5])^2`: `f(x)^T` is a static error, and `x[5]^2` compiles, but under walk fails or gives the wrong element (ledger row 1).
    97	- A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand, not a literal, because an expression of literals alone folds before the run (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
    98	
    99	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
   100	
   101	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
   102	
   103	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
   104	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
   105	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
   106	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
   107	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised, or a static error of a phase before the run, such as the disambiguator's, counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk misses: it is green while the program loads and runs clean, and red once walk refuses it.
   108	
   109	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
   110	
   111	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
   112	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
   113	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
   114	- `one_library_tests/`: a test whose program compiles against the one library, for a defect that only that library shows. Its tests compile with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, and `ant testOneLibrary` and `testFast` run them. A plain run test there runs against the one library's jars, as `OneLibraryRunHello.test` does. `compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", lists what it cannot run, and `tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests", says how to run it.
   115	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series. Put no new test there.
   116	
   117	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
   118	
   119	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
   120	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
   121	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
   122	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
   123	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
   124	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
   125	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
   126	
   127	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:
   128	
   129	    tests=EqualityRung1
   130	    link
   131	    run
   132	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
   133	
   134	## How `XXX` works
   135	
   136	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
   137	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
   138	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
   139	- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
   140	- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
   141	- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.
   142	
   143	## How a defect is recorded
   144	
   145	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
   146	
   147	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
   148	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
   149	3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.
   150	
   151	If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.
   152	
   153	## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
   154	
   155	1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
   156	2. Run the test's program through the harness before you run it any other way. In that Bash call, echo a line that starts `Expected failure:` before the harness command. In that line, say how the harness should report the failure. Then see the test fail that way through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says. If the test passes, or fails another way, find out why and correct it before you make the fix. Then echo the expected failure again in the Bash call that runs the test again. If the run meets a second defect, record it as "How a defect is recorded" says.
   157	3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
   158	
   159	The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.
   160	
   161	In your report, quote each `Expected failure:` line as the call echoed it, two to five lines of each failing run, and the passing line, each run with its command. Give the cause of each run that failed another way. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.
   162	
   163	An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.
   164	
   165	## Writing an `XXX` test
   166	
   167	In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.
   168	
   169	- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
   170	- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
   171	- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
   172	  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
   173	  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
   174	  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
   175	  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.
   176	
   177	Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. Run it twice:
   178	
   179	1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
   180	2. Changed for one run so that the defect does not show, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, set the expected string to what the run prints, or, in a run-time pair, remove the part that fails.
   181	
   182	## Promoting an `XXX` test
   183	
   184	If your change fixes a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the fix turns that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then promote it:
   185	
   186	1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv` (`committing.md` gives the commit), or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet. Rename each `XXX` name inside: the `component` line, and in a compiled test the `tests=` lines and keys. Change a run-time pair as below.
   187	2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code, as "The order", step 2, says.
   188	3. Make the fix and see the test pass.
   189	
   190	A run-time pair keeps its three files, renamed without `XXX`. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:
   191	
   192	- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
   193	- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
   194	- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.
   195	
   196	## Names, comments, citations
   197	
   198	- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
   199	- Assert each case in one test only. Add a new case to the test that already asserts cases of its kind: `git grep` for the case's name or value finds it. A case that fails today goes in an `XXX` test, since it would turn a plain test red.
   200	- Write an assertion's message as one short line that says what was checked. Put a reason that several assertions share in one comment line above them.
   201	- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
   202	- If your change breaks a line of a test that the team wrote, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Keep every assertion. List each line's before and after in your report.
   203	- If your change touches mutable state, a field, an `atomic` block, library code that writes shared state, or the Java of tasks, transactions or the class loader, run its checks at one thread and at four. `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` and the suites force four threads. For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.
   204	- Under walk, a parallel range of sixteen elements or fewer, as `0#16`, runs its bodies in index order, so a test of parallelism there needs a longer range. For the compiled path, see `compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path".

content.content:
1	# Running tests
     2	
     3	**track**
     4	: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.
     5	
     6	**shard**
     7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
     8	
     9	**code state**
    10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
    11	
    12	## The two suites
    13	
    14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,650 tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:
    15	
    16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
    17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
    18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
    19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
    20	- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.
    21	
    22	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
    23	
    24	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
    25	
    26	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
    27	
    28	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
    29	
    30	The two suites work in the same way:
    31	
    32	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
    33	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
    34	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
    35	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
    36	
    37	To run a suite:
    38	
    39	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
    40	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
    41	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
    42	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
    43	
    44	## The switches that the harness reads
    45	
    46	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
    47	
    48	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
    49	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
    50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
    51	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
    52	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
    53	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
    54	
    55	## Outside the gate
    56	
    57	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
    58	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
    59	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
    60	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
    61	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
    62	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
    63	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
    64	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
    65	
    66	## When to run a whole suite
    67	
    68	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
    69	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
    70	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
    71	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
    72	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
    73	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
    74	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
    75	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
    76	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
    77	
    78	The suites do not check these:
    79	
    80	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
    81	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
    82	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
    83	- `fortress unparse`;
    84	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
    85	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
    86	
    87	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
    88	
    89	## One test, or a few
    90	
    91	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
    92	
    93	### Interpreter tests
    94	
    95	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
    96	
    97	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
    98	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
    99	
   100	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
   101	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
   102	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
   103	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
   104	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
   105	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
   106	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
   107	
   108	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
   109	
   110	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
   111	
   112	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
   113	
   114	### Compiled tests
   115	
   116	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:
   117	
   118	- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
   119	- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
   120	- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.
   121	
   122	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
   123	
   124	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
   125	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
   126	
   127	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
   128	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
   129	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
   130	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
   131	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
   132	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
   133	
   134	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
   135	
   136	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
   137	
   138	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
   139	
   140	## One unit-test class, or one track
   141	
   142	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
   143	
   144	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
   145	
   146	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
   147	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
   148	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
   149	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
   150	- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.
   151	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
   152	
   153	**tree**
   154	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
   155	
   156	**library order**
   157	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
   158	
   159	**DSL grammar**
   160	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
   161	
   162	**parser directory**
   163	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
   164	
   165	## Setting up each call
   166	
   167	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
   168	
   169	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
   170	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
   171	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
   172	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
   173	
   174	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
   175	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
   176	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
   177	
   178	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
   179	
   180	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
   181	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
   182	
   183	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
   184	
   185	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
   186	
   187	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
   188	
   189	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
   190	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
   191	
   192	## Two layers of code
   193	
   194	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
   195	
   196	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
   197	
   198	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
   199	
   200	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
   201	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
   202	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
   203	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
   204	
   205	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
   206	
   207	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
   208	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
   209	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
   210	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
   211	
   212	## The caches
   213	
   214	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
   215	
   216	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
   217	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
   218	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
   219	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
   220	
   221	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
   222	
   223	With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, a run that names no private caches folder uses `default_repository/caches-one` in place of `default_repository/caches`, because a caches folder holds the jars of a single library. Set the environment variable, not only the property `-Dfortress.library=one`. The class path scripts, `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`, read only the variable. With the property alone, the compile writes to `caches-one`, but the run looks in `caches` and prints 'Could not load P'. Run the library order without the variable: it fills `caches` with the prelude's jars. A program compiled with the variable runs only if its caches folder holds the jars of the one library's fourteen components, which `one_library_tests/OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles. To fill `caches-one` with them, run that test with `junit.sh` and the variable (`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests").
   224	
   225	## The library order
   226	
   227	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
   228	
   229	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
   230	
   231	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
   232	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
   233	
   234	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
   235	
   236	    cd ProjectFortress
   237	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
   238	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
   239	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
   240	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
   241	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
   242	
   243	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
   244	
   245	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
   246	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
   247	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
   248	
   249	## Name resolution
   250	
   251	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
   252	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
   253	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
   254	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
   255	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
   256	
   257	## Building
   258	
   259	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
   260	
   261	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
   262	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
   263	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` and `default_repository/caches-one`, each if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
   264	- `ant cleanCache` deletes both folders, whatever their stamp.
   265	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
   266	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
   267	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
   268	
   269	## After an edit of the library
   270	
   271	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
   272	
   273	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
   274	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
   275	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
   276	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
   277	
   278	## Symptoms of a skipped step
   279	
   280	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
   281	
   282	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
   283	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
   284	
   285	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
   286	
   287	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
   288	
   289	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
   290	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
   291	
   292	Two more facts help you read a run:
   293	
   294	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
   295	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.

1	# The gate
     2	
     3	The gate runs the seven steps below on one tree, in about 25 minutes. It is green if every step passes, and red if one fails. If a step fails, run the rest, so that the summary holds every step's result.
     4	
     5	## What it writes
     6	
     7	The summary, `summary.txt`, has one tab-separated row for each suite: `track/suite`, tests, failures, errors, skipped. Below the rows, lines that start with `#` give each log's `BUILD` and `Total time:` lines, the machine that ran the gate (`# machine`), the atomic runs and the ladder's comparison. A landed summary can also end with `# microgpt-walk` lines: the `VERDICT:` and `rc=` lines of the microGPT walk check (`interpreter.md`, "The model program"), run on the landed tree. Add them only if your brief asks for the microGPT walk check on the landed tree.
     8	
     9	If your brief asks you to land a gate's results, put them in a new `gate/` folder in `explorations/compile-ladder/`, under the `climb-batch-` name that your brief gives, in the form of the newest one: `summary.txt`, and in `ladder/` the files `ladder.tsv`, `microgpt-phase.md`, `comparison.txt` and `microgpt-comparison.txt`. The next gate compares with the newest summary there or in `explorations/compile-ladder/gate-baseline/`, and finds no other. Land them in a commit that changes nothing else that the gate reads.
    10	
    11	Steps 5 and 7 use shell functions that `explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh` defines. The file runs nothing. In each Bash call of steps 5 and 7, set up the call as `build-and-caches.md` says, which sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the tree's root. Then source the file, from the root:
    12	
    13	    source explorations/coordinator/tools/gate-functions.sh
    14	
    15	## When to run it
    16	
    17	Your brief says whether you run the gate. If it does not ask, run only your own tests (`tests-running.md`).
    18	
    19	If it asks, first check whether the newest gate still holds for your tree. A gate's tables stay valid until the tree changes under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or in `build.xml`, outside the test files. A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` file directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. The commit that landed the newest summary changed nothing that the gate reads. Commit your tree, then run this command. It prints each path, test files excepted, changed since that commit:
    20	
    21	    G=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt')
    22	    git diff --name-only $G HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml \
    23	        | grep -v -E '^ProjectFortress/([^/]*_)?tests/[^/]*\.(fss|fsi|test)$'
    24	
    25	- If it prints a path, run the gate.
    26	- If not, the newest gate holds. Run only the changed test files, through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` (`tests-running.md`).
    27	
    28	## The steps
    29	
    30	Run these steps from the tree's root. Keep the logs of steps 2 and 4 in `tmp/gate/`, as `compileAll.txt`, `testFast.txt`, `testSystem.txt` and `testSpecData.txt`.
    31	
    32	1. Read the Avail column of `df -h /`. Warning: deleting `/tmp/fortress*rats` can break other live runs. If the column shows less than 1 GB, delete `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, and read it again. If it still shows less than 500 MB, stop and report.
    33	2. Run `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS tmp/gate && mkdir -p tmp/gate`, then `ant compileAll`.
    34	3. If the build printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, run the library order (`build-and-caches.md`). If not, and a source of the compiler's library changed since the caches were filled, take its step in `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library". Then copy the caches twice for the ladder regression, before anything else compiles into them:
    35	
    36	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; mkdir -p $D/root
    37	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/ladder-caches
    38	       cp -a default_repository/caches $D/root/pristine
    39	
    40	4. Run `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, then `ant testSpecData`. All three must have zero failures. In `ant testSystem`, `tests/XXXAtomicNestedReadsKeptWalk` can print `PASS` and fail with 'Missing expected failure': its expected failure depends on a race (ledger row 1004). The gate is then red, as for any failure. Cite the row in your report.
    41	5. Write the summary: `gate_summary tmp/gate tmp/gate/summary.txt`. Compare it: `gate_compare "$(last_landed_summary)" tmp/gate/summary.txt`. It prints a line for a suite with failures or errors, a suite with no tests, a suite whose count of tests fell, and a suite that is gone. Each such line makes the gate red. A count that rose prints nothing.
    42	6. Do the atomic runs, and append their lines to the summary.
    43	7. Do the ladder regression.
    44	
    45	## The atomic runs
    46	
    47	The atomic runs compile the programs below, and run each one three times at four threads. They need the library's jars in the tree's caches (`build-and-caches.md`). Run them from `ProjectFortress/`:
    48	
    49	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
    50	             AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled CallArgumentsForkCompiled AtomicOwnWriteNestedCompiled \
    51	             AtomicNestedSameBodyCompiled NestedAtomicAbortCompiled AtomicNestedViewCompiled \
    52	             AtomicSharedReadsCompiled AtomicThrowRevertsCompiled AtomicExprCompiled AtomicFieldCompiled \
    53	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
    54	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
    55	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
    56	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "# atomic $p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
    57	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
    58	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
    59	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
    60	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
    61	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
    62	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
    63	      done
    64	    done
    65	
    66	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
    67	
    68	## The ladder regression
    69	
    70	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
    71	
    72	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
    73	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
    74	
    75	A file that moved gets a mark:
    76	
    77	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
    78	- MISSING: a file with no output.
    79	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
    80	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
    81	
    82	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
    83	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
    84	
    85	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
    86	
    87	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
    88	
    89	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
    90	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
    91	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
    92	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
    93	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
    94	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
    95	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
    96	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
    97	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
    98	
    99	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). With step 3's copies, the driver skips the library's build (about 145 s).
   100	3. Compare: `ladder_compare $B $D`, then `diff <(mg_phases $B/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases $D/microgpt-phase.md)`. Append each line that they print to the summary, with `# ladder ` before it.
   101	
   102	If your brief asks for your change's own ladder subset, write your own `subset.txt`. Put in it each file whose recorded first error in the baseline's `raw/` names something that your change touched. Run them after your edit only. Compare them with the newest landed `ladder.tsv`, or with the baseline's `raw/` for a file that the gate does not run.
   103	
   104	## Comparing with an earlier run
   105	
   106	- `ant testSystem` runs in four shards, the summary's rows `system-0` to `system-3`. A shard takes the files by their place in a sorted list, so an added file moves every later file to another shard. When you compare by hand, compare only the sum of the four. `gate_compare` sums them.
   107	- In printed output, mask only these differences: the `Operation took <n>ms` line, a Java line number in a stack frame, an object's identity hash (`@` and hex digits), and a position in a library file that your change moved. In your report, list each test with a masked difference, and the kinds masked in it.
   108	- If your brief asks you to compare the interpreter tests with a base run, use the two scripts in `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/`. `count-run.sh` runs every `ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss` under walk, one JVM per test: run it once on the base commit and once after your edit. `compare-normalised.py` compares the two runs, with the last three masks above. Each script's header gives its usage.
   109	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
   110	
   111	**seeding**
   112	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
   113	
   114	**base build**
   115	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
   116	
   117	**old code**
   118	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
   119	
   120	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
   121	
   122	## Finding or building a base build
   123	
   124	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
   125	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
   126	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
   127	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
   128	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
   129	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
   130	
   131	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
   132	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
   133	      ant compileAll
   134	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
   135	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
   136	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
   137	
   138	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
   139	
   140	## Seeding a worktree
   141	
   142	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
   143	
   144	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
   145	
   146	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
   147	
   148	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
   149	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
   150	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
   151	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
   152	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
   153	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
   154	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
   155	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
   156	
   157	## Running the old code
   158	
   159	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
   160	
   161	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
   162	
   163	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
   164	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
   165	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
   166	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
   167	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
   168	
   169	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
   170	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
   171	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
   172	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
   173	
   174	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
   175	
   176	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
   177	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
   178	
   179	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
   180	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
   181	
   182	**prompt cache**
   183	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
   184	
   185	**interrupt**
   186	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
   187	
   188	**stop of the process**
   189	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
   190	
   191	**automatic permission check**
   192	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
   193	
   194	## The Bash tool and waits
   195	
   196	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
   197	
   198	- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
   199	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
   200	
   201	## Long commands
   202	
   203	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
   204	
   205	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
   206	
   207	Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.
   208	
   209	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
   210	
   211	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
   212	
   213	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
   214	
   215	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
   216	        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
   217	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
   218	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
   219	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
   220	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
   221	        done
   222	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
   223	    }
   224	
   225	If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.
   226	
   227	- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
   228	- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.
   229	
   230	## Stopping processes
   231	
   232	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
   233	
   234	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
   235	
   236	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
   237	
   238	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
   239	
   240	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
   241	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
   242	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
   243	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
   244	
   245	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
   246	
   247	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
   248	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
   249	# Toolchain and generated sources
   250	
   251	The build needs JDK 25: every javac task compiles at level 25 (`javaSourceVersion` in `build.xml`). The container's profile sets `JAVA_HOME` to JDK 21, under which the build stops: `invalid target release: 25`. The setup lines in `build-and-caches.md` set JDK 25, and say how to install it.
   252	
   253	Scala 2.13.18 and ASM 9.10.1 are vendored in `ProjectFortress/third_party/`. scalac runs through `scala.tools.nsc.Main`, because Scala 2.13 has no ant tasks. All sources compile as UTF-8.
   254	
   255	- In `compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/`, Fortress's own `Opcodes` hides `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes`. Write ASM's constants there fully qualified.
   256	- Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. TOOL is `JDK`, `Scala` or `ASM`. It prints 4 to 7 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`.
   257	
   258	## Generated sources
   259	
   260	These generated sources are committed:
   261	
   262	- `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` generates `nodes/`, `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, and `Library/FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi`.
   263	- The parser grammars generate the parsers.
   264	- `parser_util/precedence_resolver/operators.txt` generates `Operators.java`. Juxtaposition and operator precedence are resolved there, outside the parser grammars.
   265	
   266	The template parser, `parser/templateparser/`, is part of each parser made for a DSL grammar (`build-and-caches.md`). Its grammar copies each module of `parser/*.rats`, and adds `Gaps.rats`.
   267	
   268	- Edit the input, never the output.
   269	- If you change a rule in `parser/*.rats`, make the matching change in its copy. The suites check the copy on one program only (`tests-running.md`).
   270	- If a build changes a generated source whose input you did not edit, investigate it as a regression. Do not revert it as noise.
   271	- If scalac reports arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes, the generated nodes are stale. Run `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll`.
