content.content:
1	# The specification
     2	
     3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
     4	
     5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
     6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
     7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
     8	
     9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
    10	
    11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
    12	
    13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
    14	
    15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
    16	
    17	## Changing the text: the revision form
    18	
    19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
    20	
    21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
    22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
    23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
    24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
    25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
    26	
    27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
    28	
    29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
    30	
    31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
    32	
    33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
    34	
    35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
    36	
    37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
    38	
    39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
    40	
    41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
    42	
    43	## Building it
    44	
    45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
    46	
    47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    48	
    49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
    50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
    51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
    52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
    53	
    54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
    55	
    56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
    57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
    58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
    59	
    60	## Citing it
    61	
    62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
    63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.
    64	# Exploring: a question that the record does not settle
    65	
    66	The record keeps what earlier workers found, and they met many of the same questions.
    67	
    68	## The choices that are yours
    69	
    70	The curator settles every conflict and every question about a decision of the curator. Any other choice is yours only if it meets all four of these conditions:
    71	
    72	- It changes only one area.
    73	- It changes no line of the model program.
    74	- It changes no decision of the curator.
    75	- It can be undone.
    76	
    77	## Weighing the sources
    78	
    79	The type group is the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, from 2009 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the late positions weigh more. These positions are:
    80	
    81	- the exclusion rule;
    82	- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
    83	- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2009 and 2010;
    84	- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
    85	- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).
    86	
    87	The team's later work is outside the original tree. It is in these places:
    88	
    89	- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
    90	- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.
    91	
    92	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
    93	
    94	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
    95	
    96	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.
    97	
    98	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'
    99	
   100	When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.
   101	
   102	## The procedure
   103	
   104	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
   105	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
   106	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
   107	4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources"), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
   108	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
   109	6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours".
   110	7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
   111	8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
   112	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
   113	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
   114	   3. Copy the row into your report.
   115	9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
   116	10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
   117	11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
   118	    - the question;
   119	    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" says what else to note);
   120	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
   121	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
   122	12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.
   123	13. If your brief asked for a probe, commit its files as `committing.md`, "What to commit", says.
   124	# Committing and pushing
   125	
   126	**scratch**
   127	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
   128	
   129	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
   130	
   131	## What to commit
   132	
   133	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
   134	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
   135	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
   136	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
   137	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
   138	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
   139	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
   140	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
   141	
   142	## How to commit
   143	
   144	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
   145	
   146	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
   147	
   148	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.

22:**walk**
23:: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.
62:Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.
72:5. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
76:Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.
80:Each path has its own library today. With the environment variable `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `fortress compile` reads the one library instead, and a program compiled so runs once its caches folder holds the one library's jars (`references/build-and-caches.md`, "The caches"), but fails at some constructs that walk runs (`references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"). At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.
100:- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
101:- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
111:Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
126:An `exit` out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes, on both paths (ledger row 1039). Set a flag in the block, and exit after the block.
135:- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
136:- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
139:- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).
148:- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

193:- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`

references/compiler.md:151:  - A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, gives `Infinity`, as under walk (ledger row 980). Assert no value for it in a test.
references/interpreter.md:26:- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
references/interpreter.md:29:- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
references/revival-changes.md:64:So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one ("Numbers"), so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true`. A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` 0.5. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).
references/revival-changes.md:95:A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.
references/revival-changes.md:101:**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.

# Held list

## Held from his page comments on the page of `fortress-repo` changes, version 32 (2026-11-22 and 2026-11-23)

His reading, in chat at 08:3x UTC on 11-23: "I read until, but not including change 42." He sent no comment to Claude, "to batch your reading". The threads are on the page, not activated, so the answers go in chat.

- 08:30 on 11-23, change 42 (`interpreter.md`'s line that `00.5` keeps one leading zero, row 960): "Why do you keep pushing [this] forward, inflating skills with workaround instructions, instead of fixing this properly?!? This doesn't sound like something the switchover will resolve." The same principle as his thread on change 40 of 07:51 UTC on 11-08 (row 364): fix walk's defect, and do not extend the skill with walk's internal deficiencies. The coordinator's reading, not his words: stated twice, it binds the routing of every row that the skill teaches as a workaround.
- 08:27 on 11-23, change 41, the sentence that the compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`, so the second example does not compile until the switch-over: "Aren't we at switchover yet? Is this caveat still needed?"
- 08:13 on 11-22, change 41, "write `asFloat(x) = y`": is `asFloat` a free function declared for every number type, and is it in the specification? If the specification declared it on `Number`, should it stay abstract on `Number`, so that every number type must give it? Not for `=` alone: "Only if that was previously load bearing feature of Numbers."
- 07:30 on 11-22, change 41's reason of climb batch 29 (each numeral type declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`): he recalls that the compile-time numeral types have no operation such as `asFloat`; was the paragraph true when it was written?
- 07:24 on 11-22, on the page as a whole: define walk's `Infinity` properly where it is missing and needed, instead of getting it from an arithmetic overflow (his words were harsh).
- 07:19 on 11-22, change 40, the example `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)`: it reads as a type stored in Java's `byte`, but it only bounds the value, stored presumably as a `ZZ32`. How would a program declare a true `Byte` stored in `byte`, or, for the speed work, the `Float16` of Java's incubating Vector API? The mapping of the language onto the run time, which the specification probably does not address: "But we cannot avoid it, if we are to meet our goal."
- 07:03 on 11-22, change 40, "A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value": what is an `int` parameter? He knows only `nat` static parameters.
- 06:49 on 11-22, change 40, `Byte(v.asZZ32)` in the numeral coercion: he recalls that a `nat` has no methods; "This isn't what we discussed when we were specifying static numeric conversions per specification's wording." He remembers it otherwise than the skill: to be rechecked at the source, taking neither side.
- 06:35 on 11-22, change 40, `x.isInfinite`: how does the specification define infinity for the number types that have it? The skill gets an infinite value at run time from a numeral that overflows on purpose; is there no constant for it, as for zero? Why handle the compiler prelude's missing operations?
- 06:19 on 11-22, change 39 (a type without its own `=` compares by `SEQV`): "Mostly LGTM." Walk's tuple comparison should work on tuples of any length, as the specification defines it (row 923), so that the caveats go and the skill gets simpler: "This is a signal where we should focus impl. energy: increase language coherence."

## Held in chat (2026-11-19)

- 06:2x **His objection to the lists in the expected-failure step, a rule on how skills are written, for the skill writer and the coordinator's sorting of cold-read flags:** "I don't quite understand why we had to name examples of the failure types. It sounds like a recipe for ever growing rules section in a skill, whenever a new specific edge case that wasn't in the list is discovered. I find such writing style counterproductive. I guess it was triggered by and expanded to include the 'exit' as one extra condition by a cold reading… which shows exactly the fault case that's bothering me." The lists came from cold-read flags that the coordinator passed on; `references/skill-rewrite.md`'s opening paragraph already says that a rule states a principle, not a program of cases. The coordinator's reading, not his words: a flag whose fix is a list of cases is declined, or met by a principle. The step's lists were cut at once (skill writer, 06:2x).
- 06:2x **His word on the comparison of tiers: shelved.** "I don't think we need to run it any further. For me, it's settled that, at least at medium effort, Fable 5.2 does not outperform Opus 5.5 as was predicted by the chart"; "I don't think it makes any sense to be running Fable on high as a worker. We don't have a luxury of unlimited budget. If you consider the token cost multiplier against all models, it simply makes no economic sense"; "We will not be running it any more comparable ranks"; "it seems from the review it was not substantially detrimental, so no rework is needed either. Therefore, I think we are fine with the split of workers, models, and effort as we are running now." So the coordinator's recommendation of Fable workers at high effort is declined, and no more pairs are graded.

## Held in chat (2026-11-18)

- 15:4x **His rules for the worker's test and the skeptic, for the skill writer** (`fortress-repo`'s `tests-writing.md`, "The order", and the batch script's worker step 3 and skeptic steps 2 and 3): "When you are writing tests, you should be writing the test case, state what the expected failure is, then run it. If it matches your expected failure, then you can start working on the implementation. If it fails for a different reason than you expected, you need to deal with those cases." A test that fails for an unexpected reason does not meet test first. He asked whether the skeptic can check the stated expected failure from the worker's transcript (the coordinator's answer: yes, the statement's time and the run's output are both in it). The skeptic judges the diff by reading first and, since it may fix, trims the worker's code to the smallest in the surrounding code's forms, correctness first ("that seemed harmless"). No more ceremony on test cases: "If the skeptic sees ... the worker is adding some kind of safety net around the case that it is modifying, I think that's fine. We do not need to force the worker to perform some kind of ablation testing." So the coordinator's proposal of a case-by-case tie to an edited line is dropped. On the refactor of rung K's field into a parameter: "If the tests pass, we should be fine"; the class-file cache is not built unless measured ("If it's not measured as a performance critical thing, it doesn't matter").

content.content:
A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.
The type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} includes all of \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0}, and
\EXP{0/0}.
The advantage of $\mathbb{Q}^{\#}$ is that it is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#} are written as \txt{QQ}, \txt{QQ\_star}, and
\txt{QQ\_splat}, respectively.
See \secref{advanced-rationals} for definitions of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*},
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#}.



\subsection{Pi}
\seclabel{pi}

The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
floating-point value or interval value.
In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.

\subsection{Infinity and Zero}

The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.

\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
a floating-point number (discussed in
\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

content.content: - P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 and 907; the prelude's own `===` keeps row 908 until the switch-over). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`; P-171 makes two literals of one text one object. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. A program with a `value object CC64` tests it on both paths beside the review's 14 cases (F-326). Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. content.content:
\Trait{Fortress.Core.Tuple}
\seclabel{core-tuple}

The trait \TYP{Tuple} is the root of the type hierarchy for all tuple types (see \secref{tuple-types}).  No user-defined object can be a subtype of \TYP{Tuple}.  As with the type \TYP{Object}, the properties of its existing operators are those stated in trait \TYP{Any}.

%trait Tuple extends Any
%    excludes { Object }
%  toString(): String
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Tuple} \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Any}\)\\
{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \KWD{excludes} \{\,\TYP{Object}\,\}\)\-\\\poptabs
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-object}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave
\TYP{Tuple} the same algebraic supertraits as \TYP{Object}, at
\TYP{Tuple}, and said that it uses algebraic constraints to describe its
existing methods. No tuple type extends a trait, so the rule does not
refuse that declaration; it follows \TYP{Object}'s.}


\Method{\EXP{\VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}}}

The \VAR{toString} method returns a string \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{}''}}
concatenated as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item If the tuple has just one element, concatenate
\EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{tuple}''}}.
\item Concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{(}''}}.
\item For each element of the tuple, in left-to-right order,
     taking all plain elements before any varargs or keyword
     element, taking any varargs element before any keyword
     element, and taking keyword elements in the order defined
     by the type of the tuple (which may not be the sorted order):
     \begin{itemize}
     \item If this is a plain element,
 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of the element.
     \item If this is a varargs element ``\EXP{e\ldots}'',
 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{e} and
 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{...}''}}.
     \item If this is a keyword element ``\EXP{\VAR{id} = e}'',
 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{id},
 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{~=~}''}}, and
 concatenate the \VAR{toString} of \VAR{e}.
     \item If this is the last element of the tuple,
 concatenate \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{)}''}};
          otherwise concatenate ", ".
     \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
